entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12163"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Dan.10.1-Dan.10.21">Da 10:1-21</reference>. Daniel Comforted by an Angelic Vision.</title> <div sID="gen22055" type="x-p"/> The tenth through twelfth chapters more fully describe the vision in the eighth chapter by a second vision on the same subject, just as the vision in the seventh chapter explains more fully that in the second. The tenth chapter is the prologue; the eleventh, the prophecy itself; and the twelfth, the epilogue. The tenth chapter unfolds the spiritual worlds as the background of the historical world (<reference osisRef="Job.1.7">Job 1:7</reference>; 2:1, &c.; <reference osisRef="Zech.3.1">Zec 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2">2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.7">Re 12:7</reference>), and angels as the ministers of God's government of men. As in the world of nature (<reference osisRef="John.5.4">Joh 5:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.1-Rev.7.3">Re 7:1-3</reference>), so in that of history here; Michael, the champion of Israel, and with him another angel, whose aim is to realize God's will in the heathen world, resist the God-opposed spirit of the world. These struggles are not merely symbolical, but real (<reference osisRef="1Sam.16.13-1Sam.16.15">1Sa 16:13-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.22">1Ki 22:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Ep 6:12</reference>).<div eID="gen22055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22056" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12163"/><hi type="bold">1. third year of Cyrus--</hi>two years after Cyrus' decree for the restoration of the Jews had gone forth, in accordance with Daniel's prayer in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.3-Dan.9.19">Da 9:3-19</reference>. This vision gives not merely general outlines, or symbols, but minute details of the future, in short, anticipative history. It is the expansion of the vision in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.1-Dan.8.14">Da 8:1-14</reference>. That which then "none understood," he says here, "he understood"; the messenger being sent to him for this (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.11">Da 10:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.14">14</reference>), to make him understand it. Probably Daniel was no longer in office at court; for in <reference osisRef="Dan.1.21">Da 1:21</reference>, it is said, "Daniel continued even unto the first year of King Cyrus"; not that he died then. See on <reference osisRef="Dan.1.21">Da 1:21</reference>.<div eID="gen22056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22057" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but the time appointed was long--</hi>rather, "it (that is, the prophecy) referred to great calamity" [Maurer]; or, "long and calamitous warfare" [Gesenius]. Literally, "host going to war"; hence, warfare, calamity. <div eID="gen22057" type="x-p"/>

The tenth chapter unfolds the spiritual worlds as the background of the historical world ( Job 1:7 ; 2:1, &c.; Zec 3:1 , 2 ; Re 12:7 ), and angels as the ministers of God's government of men. As in the world of nature ( Joh 5:4 ; Re 7:1-3 ), so in that of history here; Michael, the champion of Israel, and with him another angel, whose aim is to realize God's will in the heathen world, resist the God-opposed spirit of the world. These struggles are not merely symbolical, but real ( 1Sa 16:13-15 ; 1Ki 22:22 ; Ep 6:12 ). 1. third year of Cyrus-- two years after Cyrus' decree for the restoration of the Jews had gone forth, in accordance with Daniel's prayer in Da 9:3-19 . Probably Daniel was no longer in office at court; for in Da 1:21 , it is said, "Daniel continued even unto the first year of King Cyrus"; not that he died then. See on Da 1:21 . but the time appointed was long-- rather, "it (that is, the prophecy) referred to great calamity" [Maurer]; or, "long and calamitous warfare" [Gesenius]. Literally, "host going to war"; hence, warfare, calamity.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12164"/><div sID="gen22058" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12164"/><hi type="bold">2. mourning--</hi>that is, afflicting myself by fasting from "pleasant bread, flesh and wine" (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.3">Da 10:3</reference>), as a sign of sorrow, not for its own sake. Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.9.14">Mt 9:14</reference>, "fast," answering to "mourn" (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.15">Da 10:15</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.8">1Co 8:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.3">1Ti 4:3</reference>, which prove that "fasting" is not an indispensable Christian obligation; but merely an outward expression of sorrow, and separation from ordinary worldly enjoyments, in order to give one's self to prayer (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.2">Ac 13:2</reference>). Daniel's mourning was probably for his countrymen, who met with many obstructions to their building of the temple, from their adversaries in the Persian court. <div eID="gen22058" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12166"/><div sID="gen22061" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12166"/><hi type="bold">4. first month--</hi>Nisan, the month most suited for considering Israel's calamity, being that in which the feast of unleavened bread reminded them of their Egyptian bondage. Daniel mourned not merely for the seven days appointed (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.18">Ex 12:18</reference>), from the evening of the fourteenth to the twenty-first of Nisan, but thrice seven days, to mark extraordinary sorrow. His mourning ended on the twenty-first day, the closing day of the passover feast; but the vision is not till the twenty-fourth, because of the opposition of "the prince of Persia" (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.13">Da 10:13</reference>).<div eID="gen22061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I was by ... the ... river--</hi>in waking reality, not a trance (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.7">Da 10:7</reference>); when younger, he saw the future in images, but now when old, he receives revelations from angels in common language, that is, in the apocalyptic mode. In the patriarchal period God often appeared visibly, that is, theophany. In the prophets, next in the succession, the inward character of revelation is prominent. The consummation is when the seer looks up from earth into the unseen world, and has the future shown to him by angels, that is, apocalypse. So in the New Testament there is a parallel progression: God in the flesh, the spiritual activity of the apostles and the apocalypse [Auberlen].<div eID="gen22062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22063" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hiddekel--</hi>the Tigris. <div eID="gen22063" type="x-p"/>

Persia--</hi>the angel of darkness that represented the Persian world power, to which Israel was then subject. This verse gives the reason why, though Daniel's "words were heard from the first day" (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.12">Da 10:12</reference>), the good angel did not come to him until more than three weeks had elapsed (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.4">Da 10:4</reference>).<div eID="gen22083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22084" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one and twenty days--</hi>answering to the three weeks of Daniel's mourning (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.2">Da 10:2</reference>).<div eID="gen22084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22085" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Michael--</hi>that is, "Who is like God?" Though an archangel, "one of the chief princes," Michael was not to be compared to God.<div eID="gen22085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22086" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">help me--</hi>Michael, as patron of Israel before God (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.21">Da 10:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">12:1</reference>), "helped" to influence the Persian king to permit the Jews' return to Jerusalem.<div eID="gen22086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22087" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I remained--</hi>I was detained there with the kings of Persia, that is, with the angel of the Persian rulers, with whom I had to contend, and from whom I should not have got free, but for the help of Michael. Gesenius translates, "I obtained the ascendency," that is, I gained my point against the adverse angel of Persia, so as to influence the Persian authorities to favor Israel's restoration. <div eID="gen22087" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 13. prince of ... Persia-- the angel of darkness that represented the Persian world power, to which Israel was then subject. This verse gives the reason why, though Daniel's "words were heard from the first day" ( Da 10:12 ), the good angel did not come to him until more than three weeks had elapsed ( Da 10:4 ). one and twenty days-- answering to the three weeks of Daniel's mourning ( Da 10:2 ). Michael-- that is, "Who is like God?" Though an archangel, "one of the chief princes," Michael was not to be compared to God. help me-- Michael, as patron of Israel before God ( Da 10:21 ; 12:1 ), "helped" to influence the Persian king to permit the Jews' return to Jerusalem. I remained-- I was detained there with the kings of Persia, that is, with the angel of the Persian rulers, with whom I had to contend, and from whom I should not have got free, but for the help of Michael. Gesenius translates, "I obtained the ascendency," that is, I gained my point against the adverse angel of Persia, so as to influence the Persian authorities to favor Israel's restoration.
entries.reader_content_plain: 13. prince of ... Persia-- the angel of darkness that represented the Persian world power, to which Israel was then subject. This verse gives the reason why, though Daniel's "words were heard from the first day" ( Da 10:12 ), the good angel did not come to him until more than three weeks had elapsed ( Da 10:4 ). one and twenty days-- answering to the three weeks of Daniel's mourning ( Da 10:2 ). Michael-- that is, "Who is like God?" Though an archangel, "one of the chief princes," Michael was not to be compared to God. help me-- Michael, as patron of Israel before God ( Da 10:21 ; 12:1 ), "helped" to influence the Persian king to permit the Jews' return to Jerusalem. I remained-- I was detained there with the kings of Persia, that is, with the angel of the Persian rulers, with whom I had to contend, and from whom I should not have got free, but for the help of Michael. Gesenius translates, "I obtained the ascendency," that is, I gained my point against the adverse angel of Persia, so as to influence the Persian authorities to favor Israel's restoration.
